planting.note: Set nursery transplants in spring into deep, loose sandy or sandy-loam soil in full sun, matching the rolling plains of the Llano Estacado where this stemless yucca is most common.

directions: Plains yucca forms a stemless, clump-forming rosette of narrow, rigid, blue-gray leaves closely related to soapweed yucca but typically shorter-leaved and more tightly clumped, suited to the sandy tablelands and shortgrass plains of the Llano Estacado and adjacent Texas Panhandle. A stout flower stalk emerges from the rosette in late spring, carrying large, pendant, cream to greenish-white bell-shaped flowers pollinated by the obligate yucca moth. It thrives in deep, loose, well-drained sandy ground and resents heavy or waterlogged soil, needing no irrigation once its taproot is established. Leave spent flower stalks in place through fall to let moth larvae complete development inside the ripening seed pods.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs in fall into lean, sandy or sandy-loam soil in full sun, mimicking the shortgrass and sand-prairie openings of the Llano Estacado where this onion is found.

directions: Plains wild onion is a small, grass-leaved native bulb of the shortgrass and sand prairies of the southern Great Plains, producing a tight rosette of thread-like leaves well below the surrounding grasses. In spring it sends up a short, leafless stalk topped by a compact umbel of rose-pink to deep-pink flowers carrying an unusually strong, sweet fragrance that gave the species its name. It is easy to overlook until bloom, then draws a steady stream of small native bees to its scented flowers, and goes dormant quickly afterward as its foliage withers in summer heat. Grow it in lean, fast-draining sandy soil in full sun and avoid rich or regularly irrigated beds, which shorten its lifespan and dilute its bloom.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, well-drained, sandy or caliche soil in full sun; this mesa and canyon-breaks native self-sows readily once a colony is established.

directions: Flaxflowered ipomopsis is a fine-textured, airy wildflower of dry plains, mesas, and canyon rims from the Llano Estacado west through New Mexico, with thread-like foliage that nearly disappears into the surrounding shortgrass until bloom. Slender, elongated, pale blue to white trumpet-shaped flowers open in loose branching clusters from late spring through summer, their long narrow throat shaped for pollination by hawk moths and hummingbirds at dusk. It favors lean, fast-draining caliche or sandy-gravelly soil and performs poorly in rich, regularly watered ground, where it becomes leggy and short-lived. Scatter seed over bare, open soil in fall and let the colony self-sow into disturbed patches for the most persistent planting.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into gypsum, caliche, or gravelly soil in full sun, matching the canyon-break slopes of the Caprock Canyonlands where this species is restricted.

directions: Reverchon's blazingstar is a compact relative of bractless blazingstar restricted to the gypsum and caliche canyon breaks of the Llano Estacado, where it roots into bare, crumbling slopes that few other wildflowers colonize. Like its wider-ranging cousin, its leaves and stems are covered in stiff, barbed hairs that cling tenaciously to fur and clothing, and its pale cream to white, star-shaped flowers open toward evening to draw in night-flying moths. The plant stays lower and more compact than bractless blazingstar, forming a loose mound rather than tall upright stems, which suits it to the rocky, wind-scoured ledges it naturally occupies. Give it the leanest, driest, most mineral soil available and full sun, and avoid any irrigation beyond establishment, since excess moisture quickly kills this canyon specialist.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; wavyleaf thistle forms a basal rosette through its first year before flowering the following summer.

directions: Wavyleaf thistle is a native shortgrass-prairie biennial of the Llano Estacado and broader Great Plains, easily told apart from invasive thistles by its densely silvery, wavy-margined leaves that give the whole plant a frosted appearance even before bloom. Rose-pink to lavender flower heads top the stems in summer and draw an outsized number of native bees, butterflies, and migrating monarchs compared to most other prairie wildflowers, making it one of the better-value native pollinator plants despite its spiny look. It forms only a ground-level leaf rosette its first year, then sends up flowering stems and sets seed the second year before the plant dies, so a self-sustaining stand needs new rosettes recruiting each season. It thrives on neglect in lean, dry, rocky or sandy soil and should never be confused with aggressive non-native thistles, since it spreads only by seed and does not form invasive colonies.
